- ‌**moirai** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Moirai.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Moirai" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Moirai ‌place ​fate, destiny, ​thread ​at ​the center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Moirai ‌appears ​in greek ‌tradition ​as fate, ​destiny, ​thread. ​The name's ​meaning, ‌"Apportioners ​(from μείρομαι)", ‌shapes ​the narratives ‌told ​about ‌this figure.

### ​Worship ‌and ​Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ‌and later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved ​Moirai in ​ritual, ‌text, ​and iconography, ​ensuring ‌the name ​survived ​into ‌the modern ​scholarly ‌record.

​The myths ​of ​Moirai survive ​in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, and ​later ‌retellings. ​Each version ​reflects ‌the interests ‌of ‌its ‌tellers — ​poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does ​not privilege ​a ‌single ​version; it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Moirai ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

overview.body:
**Moirai** ​(*moirai*) — ‌Fate, Destiny, ‌Thread ​· Apportioners ​(from μείρομαι) ​— ​belongs to ​the Greek ‌tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Fate, Destiny, ​Thread". ‌The name ​means "Apportioners ​(from ​μείρομαι)"[^1].

The ​**Moirai** are ​the ‌three Apportioners ​— Klōthō ‌the ​Spinner, Lachesis ‌the Allotter, ​and ‌Atropos the ​Unturning — ‌**who ​spin, measure, ​and cut ‌the ‌thread of ‌every life**, ​god ​and mortal ‌alike. Older ​than ​Zeus in ‌one of ​their ​two genealogies, ‌they are ​the one ‌power ​even the ​gods do ​not ​govern: fate, ‌portion, the ‌measured ​length of ‌a life.[^2]

​PuniCodex ​records the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling ‌**Moirai** and ‌serves its ​temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/moirai/). The ​displayed ​form is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form *moirai* ​contains the ‌same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sources.citation: Euripides, Alcestis 1–27; Apollodorus, Library 3.10.4; Hyginus, Fabulae 50–51 (Apollo and Admetos).

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Greek ​as **Μοῖραι**. ​Etymologically ​it ​means "Apportioners ‌(from ​μείρομαι)"[^1].

​Apportioners (from ‌μείρομαι)

​The ‌canonical ​spelling **Moirai** ‌matches ​the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. ​The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*moirai* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters, ​so ‌no lost ​diacritics ‌or ​encoding transition ​is ‌claimed. ‌The editorial ‌work ​is ​to fix ‌one ​reviewed ​reference ‌spelling, preserve ​capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ​keep ‌the ​original evidence ​visible. ​The ​displayed ‌form is ‌ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from ‌the displayed ‌form ‌itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**m** ​→ **M** ​— ‌Mu
- ​**o** → ​**o** ​— ‌Short omicron
- ​**i** ​→ ​**i** — ‌Short ​iota
- ‌**r** ​→ **r** ‌— ​Rho
- ‌**a** → ‌**a** ​— ​Short alpha
- ​**i** ​→ ‌**i** — ‌Short ​iota

meditation.body:
The ​Moirai are ‌Greek theology’s ‌quietest, most ​radical idea: ​that the ​universe has ​a budget. ​Every life ‌is allotted ​— spun ​out, ‌measured, cut ​— and ‌neither prayer ​nor virtue ‌can extend ​the thread ​by a ​single cubit, ​though in ​the *Odyssey* ‌Zeus ​protests (and ‌concedes) that ​mortals blame ‌the gods ​for what ‌their own ​recklessness brings. ‌Homer already ​contains the ​argument the ‌philosophers ‌will spend ‌four centuries ​having: is ​fate compulsion, ‌or only ​foreknowledge?

Plato’s ​answer — ‌that we ​choose our ​lives and ‌the ​Moirai only ‌hold the ​spindle — ​turns fate ​into freedom ​with a ‌terrible caveat: ‌the choice ​is made ‌half-blind, drunk ​on ​forgetfulness. The ‌Moirai thus ‌stand exactly ‌where Greek ‌thought passes ​from myth ‌to ethics. ​They ask ​the question ​every mortal ‌asks ​at three ​in the ​morning — ‌how long, ​why me, ​who decided ​— and ‌they answer ​with their ‌implements: it ​is ‌spun, it ​is measured, ‌it is ‌cut; and ​between the ​measuring and ​the cutting, ​everything you ‌are is ‌up to ​you.[^1]
